newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK CHANCES OF WESTERN INTEGRATION WANE - DIPLOMATS.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK CHANCES OF WESTERN INTEGRATION WANE - DIPLOMATS.

text.p: Slovakia's chances of being in the first wave of former East Bloc nations admitted to NATO and the EU are waning as deeds outweigh declarations of political intent, western diplomats said on Wednesday.
The EU and U.S. have long voiced concerns, and diplomatic notes, over footdragging by the government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar on democratic reforms.

But parliament's approval on Tuesday of an ammendment to the penal code, which which borrows from communist-era legislation by setting out punishments for acts such as organising anti-government demonstrations, may have been the straw that broke the camel's back.

"We have stopped issuing statements of concern over the development of democracy in Slovakia and will watch for improvements, if any, before accession talks to NATO and the European Union," one western diplomat told Reuters.
"But frankly they do not have a chance of making the first round," he added.
Slovakia is already an associate member of the EU and a member of NATO's Partnership for Peace programme. It has applied for membership both in the European Union and NATO.

NATO is to hold a summit in Madrid next July to nominate the first candidates for membership from post-communist countries and the EU will select membership candidates in the second half of next year.
Until recently, Slovakia was considered to be among first round contenders for membership in both organisations along with the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary.

"They know our political standards and that they must achieve them if they want to be eligible for NATO and EU membership," another diplomat added. "We have other priorities than to care for members' democratic problems."
Meciar and his ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS) have increasingly been the focus of western concerns over it attitude towards democratic reforms.
Since the autumn of 1994 the ruling coalition of the HZDS, the ultra-nationalist Slovak National Party (SNS) and the ultra-left Workers' Party has dominated parliament.
Together, they have rammed through controversial legislation over protests of the opposition and western governments, much of which has been ruled unconstitutional by the constitutional court.

One of the first acts of the coalition when it took power in November 1994 was to grab control of the state print and electronic media, key parliamentary bodies and committees, the state privatisation agency, the prosecutor's office and begin limiting the powers of the president.
Recently Meciar used his control of parliament to oust former HZDS deputy Frantisek Gaulieder who quit the party to protest the lack of democracy in Slovakia.

Gaulieder's mandate was lifted on the basis of a letter of resignation he denied sending, despite his two written and numerous oral statements to the contrary. Three days after his expulsion a bomb exploded outside his home.
Official Slovak reaction to western concerns has been mostly cavalier and indicating a real lack of interest in joining western structures despite official proclamations to the contrary.
Meciar said that many western statements regarding Slovakia were based on incorrect information from opposition sources.

"When these (concerns) are based on false information then these institutions should be told that they are being misled, that they have not been told the truth and that the material to which they reacting is not true," Meciar said recently.
Meciar's coalition partner Jan Slota, leader of the SNS which hold the government defence portfolio, was more open in his opposition to joining NATO and the EU.
"Joining military components (of NATO) would be a very doubtful move...What difference will it make whether Russian or American nuclear missiles point at us?" Slotha said.

"I am not essentialy against Slovakia's membership in the EU, but let nobody blackmail us all the time. If somebody thinks Slovaks will kneel at the door begging for (EU) admission, they are wrong," he added.
Western diplomats declined to directly comment Slota's statements. But one said:"It's another signal that we are closely watching."
